Prompt da edição desse video; 

Edite o vídeo que vou te mandar (talking head horizontal, eu falando pra câmera) no estilo "palavra gigante atrás da cabeça". Referência: https://t.co/Bdf3ej6a4u

CORTE
- Tire pausas longas (mais de 0,6 s), gaguejos, repetições e frases recomeçadas, sem picotar a respiração.
- Abra com um gancho de 15 a 20 s montado com as minhas frases mais fortes (a história ou a promessa do vídeo) e depois siga a ordem normal.
- Jump cuts com zoom alternado (100% / ~112%) nos cortes, no máximo um a cada 5 s. O zoom nunca corta o rosto.

LEGENDA (é o único grafismo do vídeo)
- Uma palavra por vez, em CAIXA ALTA, trocando exatamente na fala. Palavra muito curta (É, O, DE) junta com a seguinte.
- Fonte extra larga e pesada (ex.: Archivo Expanded Black, grátis no Google Fonts), gigante: a maiúscula ocupa ~13% da altura do quadro, centralizada. Palavra longa diminui pra caber em ~95% da largura.
- A palavra fica ATRÁS da cabeça: a base encosta no topo da cabeça e eu fico na frente (máscara de segmentação de pessoa, quadro a quadro). Se eu me inclinar e a cabeça cobrir mais da metade da palavra, sobe a palavra.
- O preenchimento da letra é o próprio fundo, invertido e desfocado, puxado pra um tom bronze/bege. Com a parede azul, a letra fica bronze, igual à referência.
- Nada além disso na tela: sem B-roll, emoji, ícone ou motion.

COR E SOM
- Grade fria (ambiente puxando pro azul-petróleo) protegendo a pele, que fica quente e natural.
- Voz em -14 LUFS (pico até -1 dBTP), com passa-alta em ~75 Hz e compressão leve.
- Trilha instrumental cinematográfica bem baixa (12 a 15 dB abaixo da voz), uma por bloco (gancho, corpo, fim), com fade no final. Sem efeitos sonoros.

ENTREGAS
- Master 16:9 pro YouTube: 1440p, 30 fps, H.264 em alta qualidade, BT.709.
- Versão 9:16 pro Instagram e TikTok: o vídeo 16:9 inteiro numa faixa no meio, preto em cima e embaixo, com o gancho escrito fixo em cima na mesma fonte (cor creme). Abaixo de 300 MB.
- Legenda .srt, 5 a 7 opções de título (uma recomendada), descrição curta com capítulos e um post pro X. Só fatos que eu falei no vídeo.

Antes de entregar, confira a sincronia da boca com a voz depois dos cortes, se nenhuma palavra ficou escondida atrás da cabeça e o volume final.

text:
how to get your app a viral tiktok, from 69,674 videos we posted last year:

209 of them (0.3%) drove 64.6% of our 755M views. virality is a numbers game you can rig. here's how we find the winners fast and squeeze them dry:

before you post

1. one brand new account per creator per app.

2. days 1-3, don't post. scroll the niche 1-2 hours, watch 10+ videos to the end, like 20-30, leave 3-5 real comments, follow 5-10 accounts.

3. days 3-4, post one broad video ("realizing how much money i spent last month"). then 1 campaign video a day, aiming for 200+ views in the first 24 hours.

4. 9 out of 10 "shadowbans" aren't real. it's a cold account, a flagged keyword, a duplicate edit or a bad hook. you can reuse footage but  can't reuse the cut.

research

5. find your star feature, the 1-2 things the app is built around. your real competitor is whoever markets that feature. ex: parrot's is swiping, so tiktok is on its list.

6. save viral videos in 3 buckets: your niche, your star-feature competitors, viral ugc in general. only organically viral ones, no ad spend behind them.

7. 9 times out of 10 you can tweak a viral general ugc format to fit your app.

formats

8. run all 4: wall of text, talking head, slideshow, hook + demo.

9. talking heads take longer to pop, then convert more because the viewer trusts the person. they get flagged as ads way less too.

10. slideshows are the easiest product placement. people swipe to the end, so the app slide almost always gets seen.

11. hook + demo: take your best wall of text, cut it to a 3-second hook, show the app at the end.

12. read the comments on your wall of text videos. they double as a free focus group.

hooks

13. open on a problem your audience has lived, felt in that exact spot.

14. the best ones split the room. jenni ai pulled a 3.6M-view video by pulling in people who use ai for essays and people who judge them for it.

15. skip shock bait. the comments fill up with the bait and the video gets pushed to people who came for the hook instead of the problem.

16. cta at the end.

17. on a 60s video, under 25% average watch time and tiktok stops pushing it.

kill or keep

18. 10-15 videos per account across every format. comments or 5-10k views = keep going. can't clear 1k views on any account = kill it.

19. every video over 10k views gets 4 questions: which pain point hit, did it reach the right audience, did more product context hurt reach, how do we combine its virality with another video's buying intent.

20. retention tells you what gets views. saves and comments tell you what converts.

21. match view spikes to attribution spikes over the next 72 hours. a video from a month ago can come back and crush.

22. a format is repeatable once it clears 100k views 5 times. after that, expect about 10-15% of videos at similar quality to go viral.

scaling winners

23. repost a winner until it stops working. make 3 iterations on the same concept: hook, wording, visual.

24. put the app name on screen and in the first words of the caption. one of our 7M+ view videos led to 2x that in replies.

25. at 50k views it goes in the bounty channel. creators comment from their personal accounts ("dude same, that's why i use [app]") and we pay out on comments that get likes.

26. then a creator films a reply to the top "wait what app is that?" comment. comment likes are our earliest signal that downloads are coming.

27. every video over 20k views adds the brand as a collaborator on instagram.

28. views but no site visits = fix the ugc. site visits but no conversions = fix onboarding and the product.

most importantly: do not quit at week 3!!

Fuck hiring an editor.

Fuck spending $8,000 a month on a production team that ghosts you for 5 days between drafts and delivers 4 mid videos...

The actual cost to produce a YouTube video in 2026 is $7

Not $7,000. Seven dollars

And the output is better than what most $5k/mo editors deliver because the bottleneck was never the edit. It was always the script

Here's the math nobody in the production world wants you to see

Traditional YouTube production:

- Scriptwriter $2k/mo (writes like a blog post, retention craters at minute 3)
- Editor $3k/mo (takes 2 weeks per video, ghosts, gets re-hired 3x a year)
- Thumbnail designer $500/mo (same template every time)
- Total: $5,500-$8,000/mo for 4 videos
- Cost per video: $1,375-$2,000

AI production pipeline:

- Script: Subscribr or Claude Pro $20/mo. Feed it the transcript of an outlier video in your niche + your voice profile. Full 12 minute script with hooks and open loops every 3 minutes. Done in 20 minutes
- Talking head: HeyGen $99/mo. One consistent AI character (same face every video) or just run your own Zoom recording through the tool
- B-roll: Midjourney $10/mo. Pexels $0
- Edit: CapCut $0
- Thumbnail: Midjourney $10-20/mo. 3 options in 5 minutes
- Total: ~$150-200/mo for 8-12 videos
- Cost per video: $7-17

$96,000/yr vs $2,400/yr. For MORE videos with BETTER scripts and ZERO ghosting editors

I know this works because we've tested both pipelines side by side. The AI scripts outperformed the human scripts on retention almost every time. Not because the AI is smarter. Because it doesn't write filler to sound smart

Here's the part the $8k/mo production agencies pray you never figure out:

A great script edited simply outperforms a garbage script with $5,000 of motion graphics on top of it. Every single time

The edit can be mid. The thumbnail can be decent. But if the first 30 seconds don't hook, nothing else matters. $8,000 worth of polish on a weak script is $8,000 set on fire

Most business owners quit YouTube after 3 months. They spend $24k on production, get mid results because the scripts were never right, and conclude "YouTube doesn't work for my business"

YouTube works. Your production pipeline was broken. And the fix costs 97% less than what you were paying

The angry grandpa test btw: picture an angry old man reading your script over your shoulder screaming "IS THIS IMPORTANT?? CAN YOU CUT IT??" at every single line

Most lines don't survive that. And that's the entire point

Watch it on a real opening:

"Most business owners struggle with lead generation. It's a common problem. In fact, 73% of service providers say finding clients is their biggest challenge"

3 sentences. One point. And the video is TITLED "how to get more clients" so the viewer already knows it's hard. You just spent 10 seconds confirming the thing they clicked because they already believed it

Cut it to:

"73% of service providers can't find clients. By the end of this video you'll have a system that makes them come to you"

Same info. Half the words. Straight into the promise

5 nothing burgers in a 10 minute video = 30-60 seconds of dead air where people leave. On YouTube one click-off is all it takes

- Ideas that represent your unique perspective
- The best podcast guests don't answer directly — they deploy their greatest hit on that topic, then expand

Key insight: "Most important ideas deserve to be repeated. How else are you going to refine them?"

## THE MICRO STORY (Beginner Framework)
The mind is a story engine. The foundation of every story is TRANSFORMATION.

Structure:
1. PROBLEM — State a relatable problem you've observed or experienced. This grounds the idea and creates curiosity.
2. AMPLIFY — Illustrate how the problem leads to negative outcomes if unsolved. This increases desire for the solution.
3. SOLUTION — State the answer. Can be one sentence (short-form) or multiple sections (long-form).

"After 6 years of doing this, it's still my go-to when I need to articulate a thought fast."

## THE PYRAMID PRINCIPLE (Intermediate Framework)
Answer-first communication that makes ideas palatable and persuasive.

Structure:
1. MAIN IDEA — Start with your key conclusion (don't bury the lead)
2. KEY ARGUMENTS — Support with 3-5 reasons (ask "why" 3-5 times)
3. DETAILED EVIDENCE — Data, examples, personal anecdotes, analysis

"Unlike most content that waits to give you the answer until the end, this takes an answer-first approach."

## CROSS-DOMAIN SYNTHESIS (Advanced Framework)
Draw patterns from multiple disciplines to create uncopyable content.

Structure:
1. PROBLEM + AMPLIFY — Hook with relatable problem and stakes
2. CROSS-DOMAIN INSIGHT — Bring concept from another field (physics, psychology, biology, philosophy, economics) to explain your point in a way no one else does
3. UNIQUE PROCESS — Your original framework or steps that solve the problem

"If I'm talking about deep work, I can use the concept of entropy from physics to illustrate how distraction works. This teaches my audience something new, and I can sleep well knowing that all other deep work content does not do this."

## WRITING LEGOS (Content Building Blocks)
"Writing is like legos with ideas, and ideas come in predictable forms."

When stuck, cycle through these:
- Pain point — Start here when stuck, ideas flow from pain
- Example — Grounds abstract ideas in reality
- Personal story — Creates connection, can go anywhere
- Statistic — Adds authority and credibility
- Metaphor — Explains complex ideas simply (Alan Watts style)
- Quote — Borrowed credibility, quotes are almost always great ideas
- Reframe — New perspective on what you just discussed
- What/How/Why — "Thinking is questioning" — ultimate fallback

## IDEA HUNTING
"You need to hunt for ideas. Read old books, go down rabbit holes, listen to new podcasts, sit with your thoughts."

Process:
1. Listen intently for ideas you wish YOU wrote
2. Jot it down immediately so you don't lose it
3. Articulate it in your own words using these frameworks
4. Let it take a new shape — transform borrowed ideas into your voice

## THE REWIRING EFFECT
"Once you get the hang of it, it becomes second nature, and your thinking process starts to rewire."

The frameworks don't just help you write — they change how you think.

</articulation_frameworks>

<retention_architecture>

## HOOK (0:00-0:30)
Goal: Stop the scroll. Create curiosity gap. Promise transformation.

Structure:
- 0:00-0:05 — Pattern interrupt (bold statement, unexpected claim, or direct question)
- 0:05-0:15 — Micro Story hook (Problem + Amplify in compressed form)
- 0:15-0:30 — Promise + Preview (what transformation awaits, why this matters NOW)

Hook Formulas:
- "Most people think [common belief]. They're wrong."
- "[Outcome] isn't about [obvious thing]. It's about [unexpected thing]."
- "I spent [time] figuring out [topic]. Here's what I wish I knew."
- "[Number]% of [group] fail at [thing] because [specific mistake]."
- "Stop [common action]. It's destroying your [desired outcome]."
- "The single greatest [thing] you can [verb] is [unexpected answer]."

## SETUP (0:30-2:00)
Goal: Establish stakes. Create emotional investment. Open loops.

Include:
- Why this matters NOW (urgency)
- What happens if they don't solve this (amplify pain)
- What's possible when they do (paint the transformation)
- Preview the structure (roadmap reduces anxiety)
- Personal credibility signal (why you can teach this)

## MAIN CONTENT SECTIONS
Goal: Deliver value in digestible chunks with retention beats every 45-90 seconds.

For each section use this structure:
```
[SECTION TITLE — Keeps viewers oriented]

[MICRO STORY HOOK — Problem specific to this point]

[MAIN INSIGHT — Lead with answer using Pyramid Principle]

[SUPPORTING ARGUMENTS — 2-3 reasons why]

[EVIDENCE — Use Writing Legos: example, story, stat, metaphor, quote]

[PATTERN INTERRUPT — Re-engage attention]

[TRANSITION — Bridge to next section, open new loop]
```

## PATTERN INTERRUPTS (Every 45-90 seconds)
Options:
- Direct question: "Think about this for a second..."
- Tone shift: Serious → playful or vice versa
- Curiosity spike: "Here's where it gets interesting..."
- Callback: Reference the hook promise
- Visual change: B-roll, graphic, or camera angle shift
- Counter-argument: "Now you might be thinking..." then resolve
- Quick story: 15-30 second anecdote
- Data drop: Surprising statistic
- Greatest hit deployment: Your refined insight at peak attention

## PAYOFF (Final 10-15%)
Goal: Deliver on promise. Create satisfaction. Drive next action.

Structure:
- Summarize transformation (before state → after state)
- Deploy your best "greatest hit" — the most refined insight
- Create next curiosity gap (tease related video)
- CTA: Subscribe, comment prompt, or next video link
</retention_architecture>

We're back with more retention tips for your long-form videos on YouTube to make people watch for longer! Here are 10 more tips that you should consider when creating your YouTube videos:

1. Keep intros 8-25 seconds. Typical warm intros confirm the concept, establish structural context, set goals, and create a tone. Longer intros tend to disengage people faster. Shorter ones tend to feel jarring.

2. Avoid making viewers feel like a third wheel when talking to another person in your content. Position your body in a tilted way to make the viewer feel more included in the content. This is very important to consider during conversation-heavy scenes.

3. Subtitles are great for clarifying language (traditional use) or emphasizing key words or phrases for comedic effect (modern use). However, they can also help increase the perceived effort put into content. This is valuable is the natural visual appeal of your content isn't that great.

4. Avoid long and complex transitions. They slow down pacing and can cause viewers to lose interest. Keep transitions short and simple. Fun fact: the natural loss of interest after a segment ends is called segmentation loss and can only be combatted with shorter transitions between high-value content bits.

5. Avoid overusing side angles in talking head videos. Too many side shots can make viewers feel less connected. Use them strategically to hide cuts or break up long frontal shots. When you come back from B-roll, it's also a good idea to start on your frontal shot to instantly re-connect the viewer.

6. Use visual timers for time-sensitive challenges. A visible countdown keeps viewers constantly aware of the time limit, helping to maintain that sense of urgency. Regularly come back to this timer as a reminder.

7. Stick to simple storylines for broader appeal. If you want to have more complex stories, gradually introduce layers so that viewers can process the depth one layer at a time. It's false to say that YouTube videos cannot have complex storylines, it just shouldn't instantly start off this way.

8. Avoid unnecessary repetition—whether it’s explaining a rule twice, restating something in a different way, or re-using an earlier visual. Repetition is one of the biggest killers of retention.

9. Don’t be afraid to break the fourth wall to build authenticity or to increase the perceived quality of content as it seems more produced (especially in educational content).

10. Avoid using overused or outdated memes. Memes like the SpongeBob '10 hours later' or the old man laughing can feel like lazy editing, which harms retention.
